lead: Rotate a phone and Android destroys the activity and builds a new one on a new layout. Rotation is a configuration change; the system answers it like a fresh launch, so values held only in Java fields die with the old object. This chapter shows the Bundle that carries state across, the view ids that save themselves, and the -land resource folders that give a real landscape design.
prereq: You need the activity life cycle from Unit 2 and the view tree from 3.1 Screen components and layouts, because rotation inflates a second layout tree.

blocks.text: Portrait on a 1080 × 1920 phone, landscape on 1920 × 1080. The resource qualifier changed, so Android treats this as a configuration change, like a language switch or a keyboard plug-in.

The response is drastic: onPause → onStop → onDestroy on the old activity, then onCreate → onStart → onResume on a new one. Two Activity objects exist in that sequence, never one. Every field — a counter, a list, a socket — belonged to the old object and is gone; the new object starts from its field initialisers.
Only one thing crosses the gap: a Bundle Android hands to onCreate, after onSaveInstanceState fills it.
onSaveInstanceState(Bundle outState) runs before the activity is destroyed for a configuration change. Write small key-value pairs: outState.putInt("count", count).
Read them in onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState). On first launch that Bundle is null, so test for null. onRestoreInstanceState(Bundle) runs after onStart, when the view tree exists.

Views with an android:id save their own state, but what each saves differs. EditText saves typed text, CheckBox its tick, ScrollView its scroll position. A plain TextView saves its text only if android:freezesText="true" is set. A view with no id saves nothing.
The Bundle is not storage. Keep a record id there, not a hundred rows; reload rows from your database (Unit 4).

sections.h3: Alternative resources and the escape hatch

blocks.text: Alternative resources carry the design. res/layout-land/activity_main.xml is a second layout used only in landscape: same file name, different folder picked by qualifier. res/values-land/ holds landscape dimensions or strings; res/values-sw600dp/ matches any screen at least 600 dp wide, such as a tablet. With no landscape layout Android reuses the portrait one and stretches it.

The escape hatch is android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize" in the manifest. Rotation then does not destroy the activity: onConfigurationChanged(Configuration) runs on the same object and fields survive. List both values; screenSize is needed by modern Android. Use it only for a surface you redraw yourself, such as a video player or drawing canvas. It never inflates a landscape layout.
To keep objects across rotation without that trick, use a retained fragment or a ViewModel; both hand the same instance to the new activity.

figure.caption: With no saving code the rebuilt activity starts at count = 0 and shows Taps: 0. Saving 7 in the Bundle, or declaring configChanges so the activity is not destroyed, keeps Taps: 7.

examples.question: An activity keeps an int field count and a TextView shows "Taps: 7" after seven taps. The phone rotates. What does the label show (a) with no saving code, (b) with onSaveInstanceState putting count in the Bundle and onCreate reading it back, (c) with android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize" declared?
steps: Before rotation the field holds count = 7 and the label reads "Taps: 7".
Rotation changes the orientation qualifier, so Android destroys the old activity and creates a new one.
(a) No saving code: the new object's count is 0, so the label reads "Taps: 0".
(b) count = 7 goes into the Bundle; the new onCreate reads 7, so the label reads "Taps: 7".
(c) configChanges is declared: the activity is not destroyed, count still holds 7, label reads "Taps: 7".
examples.answer: (a) Taps: 0, (b) Taps: 7, (c) Taps: 7 — only the Bundle copy or the configChanges declaration carries the 7 across.
examples.check:
taps_before = 7
no_save = 0
with_bundle = taps_before
with_config = taps_before
print(no_save)
print(with_bundle)
print(with_config)

traps: onSaveInstanceState is not called when the user presses Back or when you call finish(). It is for transient screen state only.
android:configChanges hides the problem but gives you no landscape layout, so the portrait design stays stretched.
Forgetting the null check on savedInstanceState crashes on the first launch.
onRestoreInstanceState runs after onStart, not before onCreate.
The Bundle is passed through the system: large bitmaps or long lists cause a TransactionTooLargeException. It is not a database.

quiz.q: List the callbacks an activity receives, in order, when the device rotates.
quiz.a: onPause, onSaveInstanceState (called only when the activity is being recreated or stopped, not on Back or finish), onStop, onDestroy on the old instance, then onCreate (with the Bundle), onStart, onRestoreInstanceState, onResume on the new one.

quiz.q: Why does an int field reset to 0 after rotation even though the app never closed?
quiz.a: The field belongs to the destroyed Activity object. A new object is constructed with fresh field initialisers.

quiz.q: Which resource folder holds a layout used only in landscape?
quiz.a: res/layout-land/, with the same file name as the portrait layout.

quiz.q: A screen has an EditText with id etName and a TextView filled from code. The phone rotates. Which text survives, and why?
quiz.a: The EditText text survives because an EditText saves its text by default. The TextView loses its text even if given an id, unless android:freezesText="true" is set or you store the string yourself in onSaveInstanceState.

quiz.q: A developer adds android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize" to fix a stretched landscape screen. Why does it not work?
quiz.a: The attribute stops the activity from being recreated, so no landscape layout is inflated. The same portrait view tree is re-measured to the new width.

quiz.q: When should state go in the Bundle and when should it go to a database?
quiz.a: Bundle for small transient UI state such as a counter or a half-typed name. Durable data such as orders or profiles goes to preferences, files or SQLite (Unit 4), because the Bundle is not called on Back and must stay small.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real apps use a ViewModel so one object outlives every recreation, and treat rotation as one case of process death, where Android kills a backgrounded app and restores it later from the same Bundle. Modern tooling adds SavedStateHandle, which wraps that Bundle in a lifecycle-aware object. Search for "SavedStateHandle" and "process death restoration" to go further.
